title: AI at Work: Course Completion Exam
description: Timed practice exam covering the whole series. Pass with 72% or higher to earn the course completion certificate.

questions.question: What does the spacing effect say about how practice should be arranged?
options: The same total practice time sticks better when split across several days than stacked into one long session
Longer practice sessions always beat shorter ones
Total practice time matters more than when the practice happens
Everyone learns best at the same hour of the day
questions.explanation: Spacing beats cramming at equal total time: the same minutes spread across days are retained far better than the same minutes in one sitting.

questions.question: A specific statistic in an AI answer is going into a client document. How should it be checked?
options: Ask a second AI tool whether the number is correct
Reread the answer to see whether it stays consistent
Accept it because the tool supplied a plausible source
Open the original report and read the figure there
questions.explanation: A claim is settled by the primary source, the report or record the figure actually came from. Another AI tool and the answer's own confidence are both the same kind of unchecked text.

questions.question: What four terms do you check a prompt against to brief a tool well?
options: Ask, Check, Ship, Stop
Plan, Draft, Review, Send
Prompt, Iterate, Verify, Decide
Role, Task, Context, Format
questions.explanation: Telling the tool who it is being, what to do, what it needs to know, and how to answer covers the brief. It is the most reused prompting skill on the sheet.

questions.question: Why should cleaning come before analysis in a spreadsheet task?
options: Cleaning is quick work and best finished early in the task
A tool refuses to open a sheet that contains duplicate rows
Analysis is only as good as the table, and a messy table gives wrong totals
Cleaning shrinks the file so it is easier to share with the team
questions.explanation: A tool sums what it is given without seeing the mess in it. Text rows, duplicates, and split labels turn into a total that is specific, polished, and wrong, so the table has to be fixed first.

questions.question: What separates editing a draft from reviewing it?
options: Editing improves quality, while reviewing decides whether it is safe to send
Editing is for long documents, while reviewing is for short ones
Editing checks the facts, while reviewing fixes the tone
Editing is optional, while reviewing only applies to numbers
questions.explanation: Editing is a craft pass that makes a draft better, and reviewing is a gate that checks whether its claims are safe and true. The two have different goals, so doing them together means one gets skipped.

questions.question: Why must a time-saved claim start with a baseline?
options: Without the time the task took before the change, there is nothing to compare against
Baselines are required for compliance reporting
A baseline removes the need to measure after the change
Baselines are only needed for financial tasks
questions.explanation: You measure before, then after, and the difference is your answer. Skipping the before number is the main reason time-saved claims fall apart.

questions.question: When you use AI for writing, what is the right division of labor?
options: The AI supplies the facts; you polish the wording
You supply the facts and judgment; the AI supplies the fluent first draft
The AI decides what is true; you format the result
You write everything; the AI only fixes spelling
questions.explanation: Fluency is not accuracy. The tool drafts quickly, but you own the facts, the judgment, and the final call on what ships.

questions.question: Which description best matches how a large language model produces an answer?
options: It looks up stored facts and returns the exact one that matches the question
It follows a fixed set of rules that a person wrote in advance
It predicts the next most likely token over and over, based on patterns from training
It searches a live database and copies the closest entry it finds
questions.explanation: A language model works by predicting the next most likely token, again and again. It produces a plausible sequence of words rather than retrieving a verified fact, which is why a confident answer can still be wrong.

questions.question: A well-built prompt has four parts. Which set names them?
options: Tone, length, keywords, and deadline
Role, task, context, and format
Question, answer, example, and summary
Model, temperature, tokens, and stop words
questions.explanation: Role, task, context, and format are the four parts of a complete brief. The role focuses the stance, the task says what to do, context supplies the facts, and format shapes the answer.

questions.question: What does a premortem ask you to do before committing to a plan?
options: List the tasks the plan still has to complete
Estimate the plan's total budget and timeline
Review the plan after it has finished
Imagine the plan has already failed and work back to why
questions.explanation: A premortem flips a vague question about what could go wrong into a specific answer by imagining the failure first. That surfaces risks while they are still cheap to fix.

questions.question: What makes a number a decision metric rather than decoration?
options: It is easy to collect automatically
It was requested by leadership
It is a large, impressive figure
You would actually change what you do based on it
questions.explanation: A count you would keep running no matter what it said tells you nothing. A metric matters when a change in it would make you act, such as drafting time creeping back up.

questions.question: What turns an action item into a real commitment rather than a wish?
options: It is written down in a shared document
It names the task, a single owner, and a deadline
It is discussed again at the next meeting
It is phrased as a suggestion rather than an order
questions.explanation: An action item without an owner is a wish; with an owner it becomes a commitment. A real one names the task, the person, and the deadline.

questions.question: A team wants to know whether an AI workflow is earning its place. Which three things should it measure?
options: Cost, speed, and satisfaction
Time saved, quality, and adoption
Volume, errors, and latency
Revenue, retention, and risk
questions.explanation: The three axes answer different questions: how much time the workflow saves, whether output quality holds, and whether people keep using it. Confusing them hides the real answer.

questions.question: What separates review from editing?
options: Editing improves a draft; review decides whether the draft is good enough to ship
Review is just a longer round of editing
Editing is done by a manager and review by the author
They are two names for the same step
questions.explanation: Editing fixes what is on the page; review is the gate that decides whether the draft should ship at all. You can edit a fine draft and still need to review one you never touched.

questions.question: The content is right but the shape is wrong: you wanted three short bullets and got three long paragraphs. What is the fix?
options: Verify every sentence against a source
Rephrase the original request and hope the shape changes
Name the format you want, and when it matters, show an example of it
Ask the tool to shorten the paragraphs a little
questions.explanation: The model defaults to the most ordinary shape, usually a wall of paragraphs, so a wrong format is fixed by naming the format you want and, when the shape really matters, showing an example.

questions.question: What is the central move that turns a prompt that worked once into a template?
options: Shortening the prompt so it is faster to type
Separating the parts that stay the same from the parts that change
Adding a placeholder for every detail mentioned in the task
Asking the tool to hold on to the prompt for next time
questions.explanation: A template keeps the stable instruction intact and marks only the values that differ between runs. That split is what removes the rewriting.

questions.question: Two tasks use the same tool: one drafts a summary only you read, the other sends a figure straight out to clients. Why is the risk so different?
options: Because the second task uses a more powerful model
Because longer outputs are more likely to contain errors
Because blast radius belongs to the task, not the tool, so the same tool can be low risk on one task and high risk on another
Because the first task does not really involve the model
questions.explanation: Blast radius is how much damage a wrong output can do, and it belongs to the task rather than the tool. A draft you can inspect and discard is low risk, while anything that leaves your hands and reaches others is not.

questions.question: You could write a short reply yourself in a few moments. Why might using the tool still be the wrong call?
options: Because short replies are not something a tool can produce
Because the tool would refuse such a small request
Because the tool would ask for more context first
Because prompting, reading, and fixing the output can cost more time than just writing it
questions.explanation: Using a tool is never free. For a small task, the time to prompt, read, and correct the output can exceed the task itself, so the tool is not worth using even when it can do the work.

questions.question: How is an agent different from a plain chatbot?
options: An agent is a chatbot that has been given a more impressive product name
An agent only answers a single question and never takes an action
An agent is a script of fixed rules with no model behind it
An agent takes several steps and uses tools on its own to reach a goal
questions.explanation: An agent can take multiple steps and use tools on its own, deciding what to do next. A plain chatbot only replies to what you type, which is why many products called agents are really just chatbots.

questions.question: Why does a short daily practice plan keep each session brief?
options: Because learners cannot concentrate for more than ten minutes
Because short sessions are the size that fits the spacing effect and stay sustainable over a month
Because longer sessions cost too much to schedule
Because the skill is too simple to need more time
questions.explanation: Short sessions are the size the spacing effect rewards and the size a person will actually keep up across many days. Inflating them breaks the daily rhythm that makes the skill stick.

questions.question: A chat has run long and the tool no longer seems to hold on to a key fact from the start. What is the reliable fix?
options: Start the conversation over and hope the fact carries through
Restate the fact in the current message so it is back in view
Repeat the entire conversation so nothing is left out
Ask the tool whether it still remembers, and rely on its answer
questions.explanation: Once the earliest text has fallen out of the window, the model cannot read it. Stating the load-bearing fact again puts it back in front of the model, which is faster and steadier than rebuilding the whole thread.

questions.question: What is the simplest test of whether a prompt is complete?
options: Rewrite it until it is as short as possible
Check that it names every keyword in the topic
Show it to a person with minimal context and see if they would know what to do
Send it to the tool twice and compare the two outputs
questions.explanation: If a person with little background could follow the prompt, the model can too. Confusion in a human reader is the signal that a part is missing.

questions.question: An AI answer is written in the same confident tone whether it is right or wrong. What follows from that?
options: Confident wording shows that the answer has been checked
Tone can be used to separate reliable answers from guesses
Confidence tells you nothing about whether a claim is true
Hedged answers are the ones most likely to be inaccurate
questions.explanation: The tool's voice stays flat and certain across everything it writes, including invented facts and citations. Certainty is a style rather than evidence, so the claim itself has to be checked.

questions.question: You hand the tool three sources that quietly contradict each other, and its summary reads as though they agree. What should you ask?
options: Which source is the most authoritative, so the others can be ignored?
How can these three sources be combined into one statement?
Where do these sources disagree, and what exactly does each one say?
Which single number best represents all three sources?
questions.explanation: The model's default is to produce smooth text with no visible contradictions, so disagreement disappears unless you force it out. A decision usually rests on a difference, so ask where the sources disagree.

questions.question: Why does the quality of a long AI reply tend to slip toward the end?
options: The model slows down and stops processing new text
The tool runs low on storage as the reply grows
Each token is a guess, so small errors pile up over a long reply
The model switches to a weaker mode partway through the reply
questions.explanation: The reply is built one token at a time, with each token chosen from probabilities. Over a long reply those small chances to steer slightly wrong compound, so the first half usually holds together better than the last.

questions.question: What does a team playbook cover that a prompt library does not?
options: The team's agreed standards for using AI: tone, data, and who checks output
The full text of every prompt the team has ever written and saved
A running log of how many AI tasks each person completes in a week
The current list of AI products and tools the company has licensed
questions.explanation: The playbook is the agreement about how the team works with AI. The library holds the working examples that follow those standards.

questions.question: What is a cheat sheet line supposed to be?
options: A short explanation that teaches the skill from scratch
A cue that reminds you of a skill you already know
A worked example you can study in depth
A glossary of terms to memorize
questions.explanation: Each line exists to jog a skill you already learned so you apply it under pressure. If a line needs a paragraph to make sense, it does not belong on the sheet.

questions.question: What does it mean to shift the tone of a message?
options: Change the facts so they fit the audience
Make the message shorter for busy readers
Rewrite the same facts so they land differently for a different audience
Add reassurance the first draft was missing
questions.explanation: A tone shift keeps the facts identical and changes how they read, so one set of facts can serve a client, a manager, or a project team.

questions.question: Why do good personal habits stop being enough once a team relies on a tool for real work?
options: Because personal habits are usually wrong
Because a habit travels with one person, while a policy has to travel with the team, and the tool becomes an organizational purchase whether or not anyone formally bought it
Because written policies are required by law in every country
Because tools change too fast for any habit to keep up
questions.explanation: A habit protects the one person who holds it. Once a team leans on a tool, the same choices become organizational, so the rules have to be written down clearly enough for anyone on the team to follow without you.

questions.question: The draft now looks finished. Why run a truth pass before sending it?
options: Because a finished-looking draft can still carry an invented fact, and every claim has to be checked
Because the tool will not send the message without one
Because a second pass always makes the writing shorter
Because the tool corrects its own errors when asked twice
questions.explanation: A draft can look done and still contain a confident, invented detail. The truth pass checks each asserted fact against what you supplied or your own records, and it catches the plausible error that would otherwise ship.

questions.question: Why does the order of the steps matter so much?
options: Because the tool only accepts the steps in a fixed interface order
Because the order sets the price of the model calls
Because each stage hands its output to the next, so getting the order right makes every following stage easier
Because reviewing a raw first draft is the best use of the first review pass
questions.explanation: The steps are an order of operations, not a menu. Briefing before drafting, drafting before iterating, and iterating before reviewing means each stage produces exactly what the next one needs.

questions.question: Why can a confident, specific number in an AI draft still be wrong?
options: The tool only rounds numbers when you ask it to
The number is usually right but the formatting is unreliable
The tool predicts what a correct-looking answer would be instead of computing the value
The tool removes any number it cannot verify
questions.explanation: A language model guesses the shape of a correct answer rather than calculating, so a precise-looking figure can be an invented approximation. Numbers need checking against a source you trust.

questions.question: What are the three pieces that keep AI use defensible once a whole team standardizes on a tool?
options: A written data policy, vendor evaluation, and a clear answer to who is accountable
Encryption at rest, regular backups, and periodic access reviews
A larger budget, faster hardware, and more staff training
Longer prompts, extra review passes, and server logging
questions.explanation: Responsible use at team scale rests on a data policy that says what is allowed in, vendor evaluation that says how the tool was chosen, and accountability that names who answers when something goes wrong.

questions.question: Why is asking whether your whole job is automatable the wrong starting question?
options: It is a question only a manager can answer
A job is a bundle of tasks, and only some of them suit a tool
It assumes automation always means writing code
It is too pessimistic to lead anywhere useful
questions.explanation: Almost every job mixes judgment with repeatable work. Asking which tasks qualify is narrow enough to act on, while the whole-job question has no useful answer.

questions.question: Why is 'can the tool do this?' the wrong first question when you decide whether to delegate a task?
options: Because the tool's answer depends on how the prompt is worded
Because the answer is almost always yes, which tells you nothing about whether you should use it
Because a tool's abilities change with every software update
Because money is the only factor that should decide the choice
questions.explanation: The tool can produce a draft or a list for nearly anything you describe, so a yes to can-I is nearly automatic. The better question is should-I, because it forces you to weigh the task itself.

questions.question: Which principle decides whether a step is safe to automate?
options: Automate whatever runs most often, regardless of the consequence
Automate the reversible steps and keep a human on the irreversible ones
Automate any step the tool can perform without making an error
Automate every step at once, then review the output each week
questions.explanation: The cost of being wrong is asymmetric. A reversible step that is wrong costs a little time, while an irreversible step that is wrong costs trust, so the reversible steps are the automation candidates.

questions.question: The tool keeps answering a different question than the one you intended. What is the most direct fix?
options: Edit each answer by hand until it fits
State the same need in different words so the request points the right way
Lower your expectations for what the tool can do
Repeat the same request in a firmer tone
questions.explanation: Rephrasing targets the request, not the answer. When the prompt sends the tool toward the wrong kind of response, rewording the request is what changes what comes back.

questions.question: A weekly routine has quietly stopped doing its job, though the writing still reads well. What is the most likely cause?
options: The person forgot the underlying skill
The output is fine and the complaint is imaginary
An assumption about the tool's behavior quietly changed
The task itself is no longer worth doing
questions.explanation: The habit stayed intact while a default it relied on moved. The failure shows up as output that looks polished but no longer serves its purpose.

questions.question: A colleague set up a free account with a personal email and uses it to draft real client work. What is the core problem?
options: Free tools are always slower than paid ones
A personal email address cannot receive the tool's replies
Tools only work properly with a company email address
A personally signed-up account is a consumer tool, where inputs may be reused and no company agreement protects them
questions.explanation: A tool you signed up for with a personal email is a consumer tool, even if you use it for work. Enterprise tools come with a data processing agreement and often a promise not to train on your inputs, which consumer tools do not.

questions.question: Two prompts cover the same situation. One names the client and gives an account number. The other describes the situation with no names or figures. What actually creates the risk?
options: The topic is more sensitive when it is described vaguely
The names and figures are the identifying detail, and that detail is what creates the exposure
There is no difference, since both prompts describe the same situation
The second prompt is riskier because it leaves information out
questions.explanation: The difference between safe and unsafe input is almost never the topic, it is the identifying detail. Strip the names, account numbers, and confidential figures and the same request becomes safe to paste.

questions.question: A company buys licenses for everyone and announces that the tool is available. Why is that not a rollout?
options: It skips the vendor evaluation step entirely
It hands out access without changing how people work
It costs more than a phased approach would
It leaves the tool undocumented for new hires
questions.explanation: Distribution delivers access. A rollout changes the default way work gets done, which takes sequencing, training, and controls rather than flipping a switch.

questions.question: A template has grown to fifteen placeholders so it can cover every variation. What is the likely result?
options: It produces generic output and becomes slow to fill in
It handles every case well and saves the most time
The tool rejects prompts with more than ten placeholders
Output quality rises because more detail reaches the model
questions.explanation: Flexibility crowds out the specific instruction that made the prompt good. Reusability is not universality, and a template that does one task well beats one that does ten poorly.

questions.question: What turns a single prompt into a workflow?
options: Running the same prompt more than once
A fixed sequence of steps, run in order, that feeds a recurring result
Using a more capable model
Saving the prompt somewhere you can find it again
questions.explanation: A prompt is one request, while a workflow is several steps arranged so each one hands its output to the next. The order and the handoffs are what make it a routine.

questions.question: What makes a working session 'end to end' rather than a piece of the task?
options: You use every feature the tool offers in one sitting
You complete the full deliverable another person will use, staying in control at every step
You run the whole thing through a single prompt
You spend an entire workday with the tool open
questions.explanation: An end-to-end session takes one task all the way to the finished deliverable another person relies on, with you in control throughout. It is not a fragment of the work or a first draft.

questions.question: You ask for help and get back a wall of generic paragraphs that could apply to any team and any project. What fixes it?
options: Verify every number against a primary source
Drop the output and start over in a different tool
Ask the tool to make its tone more confident
Complete the brief with the role, the task, the context, and the format
questions.explanation: Generic output is the signature of a vague ask. The model falls back on the most ordinary version of what you might mean, so the fix is to complete the brief: say who is talking, what to produce, what facts to use, and what shape the answer takes.

questions.question: Before you send an AI-written draft, what must you check most closely?
options: Any number, date, or commitment the draft added that you did not supply
Whether the greeting and sign-off match your usual style
Whether the draft is long enough to feel complete
Whether the opening line reads smoothly
questions.explanation: A good draft can hide an invented detail inside a paragraph that otherwise reads perfectly, so unsupplied specifics are the first thing to cut or verify.

questions.question: Why does a written quality bar beat a shared sense of what looks good?
options: Because it lets reviewers skip checking low-priority work
Because a written bar turns a drifting, feeling-based check into a fixed list
Because it removes the need for an accountable owner
Because written standards are required by compliance rules
questions.explanation: Without a written standard, what gets noticed drifts with mood and deadline. A bar makes the check the same list for everyone, so a miss points back to the standard.

questions.question: When you paste text into a public AI tool, what should you assume about it?
options: The vendor cannot see it, because the connection is private
It is deleted the moment the answer appears
It may be stored by the vendor and used to improve the product
Only you will ever be able to read it again
questions.explanation: The safe default is to treat anything you type as something the vendor could read and, depending on the tool, use later. Consumer tools often reuse conversations to train their models unless you change the setting.

questions.question: Why does adding context improve the output?
options: It helps the tool aim at the specific answer instead of a generic average
It makes the tool remember your preferences permanently
It shortens the output by removing unnecessary detail
It lets the tool choose the goal for you
questions.explanation: Left blank, context makes the tool default to the most common version of your request. Filled in with your facts, audience, and purpose, it can target the answer you actually want.

questions.question: Why is a well-edited draft not necessarily safe to ship?
options: Editing makes the text harder to read
Reviewing usually makes a draft worse
Editing changes how the draft reads without checking whether its claims are true
Editing is not a real skill
questions.explanation: Editing improves the surface of a draft, and a draft can read beautifully while still being wrong. That is why it needs a separate pass that checks the facts before it goes anywhere.

questions.question: What is an exception rule in a review process?
options: A rule that exempts managers from review
A rule that auto-approves any draft passing a quick first check
A written trigger for when output needs a second set of eyes, such as anything that states a price or a date
A rule that lets the tool skip the bar for internal work
questions.explanation: An exception rule names the triggers, like a price or a promised date, that require more than one person to look before the output ships, so the decision is settled in advance.

questions.question: What best describes an AI hallucination?
options: Output that sounds plausible but is factually wrong, irrelevant, or entirely fabricated
A grammar error that is easy to spot from the broken sentence
A rare glitch that only affects obscure trivia questions
A temporary outage that clears up when you retry the request
questions.explanation: A hallucination is not a crash or an obvious mistake. It is fluent, confident output that is wrong or invented, which is exactly what makes it easy to miss.

questions.question: What is the most effective move to make an AI tool reliable for research on a specific question?
options: Ask it what the industry generally says about the topic
Give it the actual documents to work from instead of asking it to recall
Ask for a longer and more detailed summary
Let it search the web on its own and report what it finds
questions.explanation: The biggest lever is grounding the tool in your own sources. When the documents are in front of it, the answer comes from that material instead of from what the model happens to remember.

questions.question: Which sign tells you a step has been automated too far?
options: The step runs on a schedule instead of on demand
The step produces a draft you still have to read
The step uses a saved prompt rather than a fresh one
You find yourself approving its output without actually reading it
questions.explanation: Approving output without reading it means the human check has quietly disappeared, which is the danger automation creates. The cure is to demote that step back to human-in-the-loop until you are genuinely checking it.

questions.question: When comparing options, what is the honest way to weigh a tradeoff?
options: Compare only the total cost of each option
Pick whichever option feels safest and move on
Ask what each option costs, risks, and assumes
Go with whichever option the tool recommends first
questions.explanation: Every real option costs something, risks something, and assumes something. Naming all three is what makes the comparison real instead of trusting a gut pick.

questions.question: A number appears in the tool's synthesis that was not in any document you provided. What should you do with it?
options: Use it, because the tool reads the sources faster than you can
Ask the tool to make the number more precise
Treat it as a fair average of what the sources imply
Drop it, and use only claims that trace to a source you gave
questions.explanation: Every claim you use should point to a source you provided. A number the tool introduced on its own is unverified, so it comes out until you can find it in an actual source.

questions.question: Why do shared prompts need named owners and version numbers?
options: So usage can be metered and billed back to each team
So the library can be audited for tool compliance
Because one private tweak can break a prompt for everyone, with no way back
Because version numbers make a prompt run more reliably
questions.explanation: The more people who touch a shared prompt, the easier it is for one local edit to damage it for the rest. An owner and a version keep that damage visible and reversible.

questions.question: Why is a vague claim harder to handle than a specific one?
options: Vague claims tend to be longer and harder to shorten
A vague claim cannot be tested, so a wrong one passes unnoticed
Specific claims are almost always accurate
Vague claims are the tool's way of admitting it does not know
questions.explanation: A specific claim gives you a handle, such as a number, a date, or a named source. A vague claim offers nothing to test, so it survives even when it is wrong.

questions.question: What separates a model from plain automation when you are deciding how to handle a task?
options: Automation follows rules written in advance, while a model handles situations where those rules cannot be written
Automation handles unpredictable situations, while a model only follows fixed rules
A model and automation are two names for the same kind of tool
A model returns the same answer to the same input every time, while automation varies
questions.explanation: Automation runs on rules a person wrote beforehand, and a model produces answers for situations nobody pre-coded. That is why a model is used where the work needs judgment, and why its output has to be checked.

questions.question: What turns a meeting from a wandering conversation into a plan?
options: A clear agenda set before it starts
Inviting more people into the discussion
Shortening every meeting to fifteen minutes
Recording every meeting by default
questions.explanation: A clear agenda turns a wandering conversation into a plan, and it is the most common answer people give when asked what makes a meeting work. Without one, the meeting drifts and the outcome is whatever the loudest voice wanted.
